title: Concentration & dilution
examples: What is the difference between molarity and molality?
How do I calculate the final concentration after mixing solutions?
When should I use the formula m1v1=m2v2?

explain.say: Today we will learn about solution concentration. Concentration tells us how much solute is in a solvent.
We can measure concentration using moles per cubic decimetre. This unit is written as mol per dm cubed.
Another way to measure is grams per cubic decimetre. This tells us the mass of solute in a volume.
When we dilute a solution, we use the formula m one v one equals m two v two. This keeps the moles the same.
For example, if you take one mole in one decimetre cubed, and you double the volume, the concentration halves.
In real life, making weak tea shows this idea. You start with strong tea and add more water to dilute it.

faq.q: What is the difference between molarity and molality?
faq.a: Molarity uses volume in decimetres cubed. Molality uses mass of the solvent in kilograms.
asks: Which one do I use more often?

faq.a: Yes, this formula is used specifically when you are diluting a solution by adding solvent.
asks: Can I use this for mixing two solutions?
What if I change the temperature?

faq.q: What does 'm' stand for in the formula?
faq.a: The 'm' stands for the molarity, which is the concentration of the solution.
asks: What units must the molarity be in?

faq.q: If I double the volume, what happens to the concentration?
faq.a: If you only add solvent, doubling the volume will halve the original concentration.
asks: Does volume and concentration relate inversely?
If I increase volume by three times, what happens?

faq.q: Do I need to convert units before using the formula?
faq.a: Yes, you must make sure all your units match the units required for the formula.
asks: What if I have millilitres instead of decimetres cubed?
Do I convert moles to grams first?

facts: Molarity is defined as moles of solute per cubic decimetre.
Dilution means adding more solvent to a solution.
The formula m₁v₁ = m₂v₂ helps calculate new concentrations.
If you double the volume, the concentration is halved, assuming no solute is added.

quiz.say: A chemist starts with 2 moles in 1 litre. If she dilutes it to 10 litres, what is the new concentration?
quiz.why: You must keep the total moles constant, so 2 moles in 10 litres is 0.2 mol/dm³.

wrong.0: This mistake happens if you forget to change the volume in the calculation.
wrong.2: This mistake happens if you multiply the initial concentration by the new volume.
wrong.3: This mistake happens if you divide the initial concentration by the new volume.

quiz.say: A solution has a concentration of 50 grams per decimetre cubed. If you dilute 2 litres of this to 10 litres, what is the final mass concentration?
quiz.why: The total mass of solute remains the same, so the concentration is reduced by a factor of ten.

wrong.0: This mistake happens if you multiply the initial concentration by the new volume.
wrong.1: This mistake happens if you divide the initial concentration by the new volume.
wrong.2: This mistake happens if you incorrectly calculate the total mass of solute.

quiz.say: If you mix 50 millilitres of a 4 mol/dm³ solution with enough water to make 500 millilitres, what is the final concentration?
quiz.why: The initial moles are 0.2 mol, spread over 0.5 litres, giving 0.4 mol/dm³.

wrong.0: This mistake happens if you only use the volume ratio without considering the initial concentration.
wrong.2: This mistake happens if you ignore the dilution step and use the starting concentration.
wrong.3: This mistake happens if you divide the initial concentration by the total volume.
